title: Ictal EEG changes in the piriform cortex during invasive diagnostics
summary:
What we want to investigate in this study:
We want to find out what role a small area of the brain called the piriform cortex (which is part of the olfactory center) plays in the occurrence of epileptic seizures.
To do this, we use invasive EEG measurements. This means that very fine electrodes are placed directly in the brain to measure the electrical signals there—more accurately than with the usual EEG electrodes, which are only placed on the outside of the head. The data we collect with these electrodes gives us a precise view of when and where in the brain a seizure begins and spreads.
We look in our electronic patient records for adult patients who have already undergone an invasive EEG. These individuals had an electrode inserted into the piriform cortex—we only do this if we suspect from normal (non-invasive) examinations that this area of the brain is either the trigger for the seizure or is involved very early on in the transmission of the seizure.
If we understand how the piriform cortex is involved in seizures, we will be better able to decide which areas of the brain should be removed or treated during surgery. This may lead to more effective treatment of seizures with fewer side effects.

interventions.name: Retrospective analysis of all patients who underwent implantation of deep electrodes in the piriform cortex between 2020 and 2024 at our center (Clinic and Polyclinic for Epileptology, or Clinic and Polyclinic for Neurosurgery at the University Hospital Bonn) as part of invasive pre-surgical seizure

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
- Patients who underwent invasive pre-surgical seizure diagnostics at our center (Clinic for Epileptology or Clinic for Neurosurgery at the University Hospital Bonn) between 2020 and 2024 and who had deep electrodes implanted in the piriform cortex.
Exclusion criteria:
- under 18 years of age
- no deep electrodes implanted in the piriform cortex
